    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\bun.exe OR *\\Bun.exe OR *\\BUN.EXE OR */bun) @ParentImage:(*\\python.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR */python3 OR */pip3)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\bun(\.exe)?$/i
| ParentBaseFileName=/^(python|python3|pythonw|pip|pip3)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="bun.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bun") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="bun.exe" OR Processes.process_name="bun") AND (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Hades PyPI startup hook: malicious -setup.pth dropped in site-packages AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Hades persistence/trigger artifact independent vendors confirmed — a '*-setup.pth' file planted in Python site-packages/dist-packages that executes at interpreter startup to fetch the Bun runtime. .pth files run any line beginning with 'import', so a campaign-named setup.pth is an on-startup code-execution hook that SCA scanners never inspect. Rationale: Adds the '*-setup.pth' startup-hook artifact that Socket.dev/JFrog/The Hacker News independently tied to the Hades wave (the article only names __init__.py); .pth-in-site-packages with a campaign naming convention is a high-fidelity, low-FP file signal. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave • https://thecybersecguru.com/news/hades-pypi-malware-miasma-supply-chain-attack/ • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/
ATT&CKT1546 T1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate package whose distribution genuinely ships a '<name>-setup.pth' (rare but possible for editable installs)
  • setuptools/pip writing __editable__.*.pth or distutils-precedence.pth during normal installs
  • Virtualenv creation copying a base-environment .pth into a new site-packages
  • In-house package using a .pth for namespace path configuration
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("distutils-precedence.pth","__editable__.pth") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe") and FileName startswith "__editable__")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the .pth file — a benign one contains only directory paths; the Hades variant has an 'import ...' one-liner that decodes/execs and reaches out for Bun. Note the package name embedded in the filename. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, delete/quarantine the .pth, and rotate npm/PyPI/cloud tokens for that developer. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC 'python spawns Bun' on the same host around startup; query DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory / pip freeze across the fleet for the offending package and block the version at your PyPI proxy.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where FolderPath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName endswith "-setup.pth"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("site-packages","dist-packages")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Hades PyPI - Malicious setup.pth Startup Hook in site-packages
id: c5f3e4d6-7d80-49ca-be23-4f5a6b7c8d9e
description: Detects creation of a '*-setup.pth' file in Python site-packages/dist-packages, the Hades worm's interpreter-startup code-execution hook that fetches the Bun runtime.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/miasma-and-hades-are-spreading-now-detect-them-on-developer-machines-with-suspicious-files
  - https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1546
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    FileName|endswith: '-setup.pth'
    FolderPath|contains:
      - 'site-packages'
      - 'dist-packages'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*-setup.pth OR *-setup.PTH OR *-SETUP.PTH) @TargetFilename:(*site-packages* OR *dist-packages*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/-setup\.pth$/i
| regex("(site-packages|dist-packages)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*-setup.pth" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*dist-packages*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*-setup.pth" AND (Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*dist-packages*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Worm propagation: burst of npm/PyPI publishes from a developer machine AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the self-replication stage — once Miasma/Hades steals npm/PyPI publishing tokens it republishes infected versions of every package the token can publish. A developer endpoint emitting many 'npm publish' or 'twine upload' invocations in a tight window is automated mass-republish behaviour, not human activity. Thresholded so a normal one-off release won't fire. Rationale: Targets the worm's defining self-replication behaviour described in the article (steal publish tokens, republish every package the token allows) as a publish-burst threshold; cross-checked against JFrog/Socket reporting that the same actor mass-republished across npm and PyPI. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-redhat-cloud-services/ • https://socket.dev/blog/shai-hulud-descends-to-hades-miasma-pypi-wave • https://phoenix.security/miasma-azure-hades-pypi-supply-chain-worm-2026/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A release engineer running a monorepo/Lerna/changesets publish that pushes many packages at once
  • CI release pipeline executing on a developer's machine instead of a build agent
  • Bulk version bump + publish during a coordinated multi-package release
  • Internal tooling that publishes a fleet of private scoped packages on each merge
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("build","ci","runner","release") or AccountName in~ ("svc-release","build-agent"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Review the SampleCmds — confirm whether this was an intended coordinated release (check change tickets / release calendar) and which registry/scope was targeted; legitimate bulk releases come from a known release owner on a known host. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, immediately revoke the npm/PyPI publish tokens used, force-unpublish/yank the just-published versions, and isolate the host. 3) HUNT: Pull this host's UC 'python spawns Bun' / 'suspicious config files' hits to find the infection vector; enumerate every package the leaked token can publish and audit those for tampered versions in the last 24h.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "publish" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","npm-cli.js","twine")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize PublishCount = count(), SampleCmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where PublishCount >= 5    // 5+ publishes in 10 min = automated mass republish; a human dev publishes 1-2
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "publish" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","npm-cli.js","twine")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| summarize PublishCount = count(), SampleCmds = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where PublishCount >= 5    // 5+ publishes in 10 min = automated mass republish; a human dev publishes 1-2
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*publish* (@CommandLine:*npm* OR @CommandLine:*twine*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("publish", field=CommandLine)
| (regex("npm", field=CommandLine) OR regex("twine", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count(as=PublishCount))
| PublishCount >= 5
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process="*twine*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 5
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*publish*" AND (Processes.process="*npm*" OR Processes.process="*twine*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where count >= 5
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

logsource:

    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'

            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or SHA1 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966") or MD5 in~ ("dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["dc48b09b2a5954f7ff79ab8a2fd80202bd3b59c08c7cdbc6025aa923cb4c0efe", "e1342a80d4b5e83d2c7c22e1e0aaa95f2d88e3dbf0d853a4994b180c93a4b17d", "c539766062555d47716f8432e73adbe3a0c0c954a0b6c4005017a668975e275c", "7069e28a5806db4ab0273639667d203f5e31b401d403af7e36d9f360c1f6d655", "b86c5ae9e95bd841a595440faa3eb6317441e746f241ae8fd641ab59ed1d1966"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["f7d335205b8d7b20208fb3ef93ee6dc817905dc3ae0c10a0b164f4e7d07121cd", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

From package to postinstall payload: Inside the Mastra npm supply chain compromise by Sapphire Sleet

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-18 14 use cases 9 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A poisoned npm package infected 140+ projects with a hidden payload. This report highlights how to detect, hunt, and defend against supply chain attacks using Microsoft Defender and actionable threat intelligence. The post From package to postinstall payload: Inside the Mastra npm supply chain compromise by Sapphire Sleet appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Sapphire Sleet npm postinstall dropper: node executing easy-day-js setup.cjs AIInstallation High
Hunts the Mastra supply-chain postinstall hook where npm spawns Node.js to run the easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs --no-warnings) on any workstation or CI/CD runner that ran npm install/update after the poisoned versions. Article-specific because it anchors on the typosquat package name and the exact dropper filename, not generic node execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact dropper filename (setup.cjs), the typosquat package name (easy-day-js) and the executing interpreter (node), all named verbatim in the weaponized package.json and Microsoft's own hunting query (Code Block 1). The combination is high-fidelity; neither string appears in benign node workloads together. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-links-mastra-ai-supply-chain-attack-to-north-korean-hackers/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or malware analysts intentionally detonating easy-day-js in a sandbox VM
  • An internal package legitimately named with 'setup.cjs' as its own postinstall build script (native-addon builds via node-gyp/prebuild-install)
  • EDR/CI test harnesses that replay the IOC for detection validation
  • A developer who pinned the package pre-disclosure and is reproducing the issue for remediation
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "setup.cjs" and not (ProcessCommandLine has "easy-day-js") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp", "prebuild-install"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the FolderPath/working dir resolves to a node_modules/easy-day-js path and check InitiatingProcessCommandLine for npm install/ci. Pull the SHA256 of setup.cjs and compare to the article hashes. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host/runner, kill the node process tree, and rotate every credential/token reachable from that environment (npm tokens, cloud keys, CI secrets, SSH keys) since the payload runs with the developer's full context. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (C2 to 23.254.164.92/.123), UC3 (NvmProtocal Run key), UC4 (.pkg_logs marker) and UC5 (second-stage from NodePackages) on the same DeviceId, and sweep package-lock.json across the org for easy-day-js@1.11.22 and @mastra deps published with the v1.13.1-class anomaly.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.cjs", "easy-day-js")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "node"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.cjs", "easy-day-js")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects Node.js executing the easy-day-js setup.cjs postinstall dropper from the Mastra npm supply chain compromise

Mastra easy-day-js C2 beacon to 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from any host to the two Sapphire Sleet C2 endpoints used by the easy-day-js dropper to fetch the second-stage wallet-stealer/RAT (GET 23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878 and the 23.254.164.123:443 secondary). Article-specific via the hardcoded C2 IPs decoded from the obfuscated string table. Rationale: Both IPs are decoded directly from the dropper's obfuscated string table in the article (23.254.164.92:8000 primary download URL /update/49890878, and 23.254.164.123:443 secondary C2). Hardcoded attacker IPs are the highest-fidelity IOC available; any contact is presumed malicious. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://orca.security/resources/blog/mastra-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform or sandbox sandboxing the sample and reaching the live C2
  • A SOAR/enrichment connector actively probing the IOC IPs for reachability
  • Vulnerability scanner sweeping the /24 (23.254.164.0/24, Hostwinds hosting range) that happens to touch these IPs
  • Shared NAT egress IP attribution making it hard to identify the true originating host (verify InitiatingProcessFileName is node)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("thor.exe", "nessus.exe", "nuclei.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine for the connection — confirm it is node executing setup.cjs or a NodePackages .js. Note whether the request hit :8000 (payload download) or :443 (secondary C2). 2) CONTAIN: Block 23.254.164.92 and 23.254.164.123 at perimeter/EDR, isolate the host, and capture the on-disk second stage before reimage. 3) HUNT: Correlate the connection time with UC1 (postinstall) and UC5 (detached node) on the same DeviceId; sweep proxy/firewall and DNS for any host in the org that resolved or connected to the Hostwinds C2 range, and rotate all secrets exposed on affected build environments.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

easy-day-js persistence: NvmProtocal Run key / ProgramData NodePackages autostart AIInstallation High
Hunts the Windows persistence the second stage establishes: an HKCU CurrentVersion\Run value named 'NvmProtocal' and/or autostart data pointing at C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\. Article-specific via the exact, attacker-chosen artifact name (a deliberate 'nvm'/'protocol' misspelling) and drop directory from the persistence matrix. Rationale: Uses the persistence matrix verbatim: the artifact name 'NvmProtocal' (an attacker misspelling of nvm/protocol) and the drop directory 'NodePackages'. Both are non-standard and not produced by the legitimate nvm tool, dayjs, or Node itself, making them low-FP autostart anchors. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-iocs-and-response-runbook
ATT&CKT1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool that coincidentally writes a Run value containing the substring 'NodePackages' (rare)
  • Backup/migration software replaying an old HKCU\Run hive that contains a pre-existing infection artifact
  • Detection-engineering validation that writes the NvmProtocal value into a Run key on a test host
  • Golden-image build that captured a compromised profile (investigate, do not allowlist)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full RegistryValueData to recover the second-stage path (expected C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\<random>.js) and confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is node. 2) CONTAIN: Delete the NvmProtocal Run value, remove the C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\ contents after capturing copies for IR, isolate the host, and rotate the user's credentials/tokens. 3) HUNT: Check macOS (~/Library/NodePackages/com.nvm.protocal.plist LaunchAgent) and Linux (~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/nvmconf.service) equivalents across the fleet, and correlate to UC1/UC2/UC5 on the same host to establish the full chain.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryValueName =~ "NvmProtocal" or RegistryValueData has "NodePackages"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryValue =~ "NvmProtocal" or RegistryValueData has "NodePackages"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js install markers: .pkg_history / .pkg_logs dropped by Node.js AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the dropper's filesystem tracking markers — $TMPDIR/.pkg_history (compromised package install path) and $TMPDIR/.pkg_logs (package name XOR-0x80 encoded) — written by the node process during the postinstall phase. Article-specific via the exact marker filenames written by the Node.js dropper. Rationale: The two marker filenames (.pkg_history, .pkg_logs) are decoded verbatim in the article (the .pkg_logs XOR-0x80 marker resolves to 'easy-day-js'). Scoping the writer to node and the filenames to these two strings makes it a clean, low-volume hunt for any infected install — including ones where C2 was unreachable. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1027 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign package manager or build tool that writes dotfiles named .pkg_history/.pkg_logs to temp (uncommon; verify the writer is node and the path is the OS temp dir)
  • Forensic tooling restoring the markers during IR replay on a clean host
  • Security validation harness dropping the IOC files for rule testing
  • Backup agents copying the temp dir of a previously infected user profile
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read .pkg_history to recover the install path of the compromised node_modules package, and confirm InitiatingProcessCommandLine shows setup.cjs / npm install. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the node tree, and treat the workstation/runner secrets as exposed — rotate npm/cloud/CI tokens. 3) HUNT: Even if no C2 (UC2) fired, sweep for the persistence artifacts (UC3) and second-stage process (UC5) on the same host, and grep the org's lockfiles for easy-day-js@1.11.22 and @mastra packages republished around the v1.13.1 anomaly window (2026-06-16/17).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ (".pkg_history", ".pkg_logs")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (".pkg_history", ".pkg_logs")
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js second stage: detached Node.js executing .js from ProgramData NodePackages AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the second-stage execution where the dropper (node) spawns a fully detached, window-hidden child node process running a randomly named .js written under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\. Article-specific via the node→node parent/child chain plus the unique NodePackages drop directory, surfacing the random script via the command line rather than hardcoding it. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described execution shape (dropper-node spawns a detached hidden node running a randomly named .js) plus the NodePackages drop directory from the persistence matrix. Rather than hardcoding the random filename, it surfaces the full command line so the analyst recovers the script path; node-spawning-node into ProgramData is rare in benign workloads. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://orca.security/resources/blog/mastra-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/microsoft-links-mastra-ai-supply-chain-attack-to-north-korean-hackers/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Node application installed under C:\ProgramData that uses a child_process to run helper .js scripts (verify the parent is node and the path component is literally NodePackages)
  • Electron/CLI tools bundling their runtime under ProgramData and forking worker scripts
  • Internal build tooling that nests node invocations and references a 'NodePackages' cache directory
  • Developer reproducing the infection chain in a controlled VM
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp", "electron-builder") and FolderPath has "Program Files")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: From the matched command line recover the random .js path under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\, hash it, and compare to the article's second-stage SHA256s; confirm the parent node lineage traces back to setup.cjs (UC1). 2) CONTAIN: Kill the detached node process, isolate the host, quarantine the NodePackages directory, and rotate all reachable credentials and wallet/crypto secrets (second stage is a wallet stealer/RAT). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the second-stage hash across the fleet, check the NvmProtocal/LaunchAgent/systemd persistence (UC3), and review network telemetry (UC2) for follow-on C2 beyond the two known IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe", "node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "NodePackages" and ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "node"
| where ParentProcessName has "node"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "NodePackages" and TargetProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

DeviceFileEvents

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Blind XXE / SSRF: FHIR Java process fetches external DTD or XSLT stylesheet — CVE-2026-55471 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the exploitation side-effect of the unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory: with ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/STYLESHEET unset, the parser resolves external DTDs and stylesheets, so the FHIR/Java server makes an outbound request to an attacker URL ending in .dtd/.xsl/.xslt. Backend FHIR servers rarely fetch remote stylesheets, making this high-signal. Rationale: Anchored on the article's root cause — saxonTransform resolving external DTD/stylesheet because ACCESS_EXTERNAL_DTD/STYLESHEET are unset — expressed as a java-process / proxy egress to a .dtd/.xsl/.xslt URL, with public-DTD hosts (w3.org/oasis) filtered to cut benign XSLT toolchains. Falcon/Datadog fall back to java→public-IP since FDR/Sysmon network events carry no URL path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/ca.uhn.hapi.fhir/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/CVE-2026-55471/ • https://saxonica.plan.io/issues/4729
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Java applications legitimately fetching remote XSLT stylesheets for report rendering
  • Document/IG publishing pipelines resolving public DTDs (already filtered for w3.org/oasis/docbook)
  • Internal CI servers running XSLT transforms against an internal artifact repo over HTTP
  • RemoteUrl unpopulated by Defender when web content filtering is off, causing under-detection rather than FP
Suppression filter
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("w3.org","oasis-open.org","docbook.org","xml.org"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the destination host/URL and whether it is attacker-controlled (new domain, raw IP, recently registered); confirm the initiating process is the FHIR/Java service and correlate to a preceding inbound XML POST (UC 1). 2) Contain: block the destination at egress proxy/firewall and isolate the FHIR host if the fetched resource looks like an attacker DTD; capture the JVM's outbound connection list. 3) Hunt: check DeviceFileEvents on that host for java.exe reads of sensitive paths (file:// general-entity disclosure) and run the DNS-callback UC for parameter-entity OOB exfil.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl has_any (".dtd",".xsl",".xslt")
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("w3.org","oasis-open.org","docbook.org"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any (".dtd",".xsl",".xslt")
| where not(Url has_any ("w3.org","oasis-open.org","docbook.org"))
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and not(ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

XXE parameter-entity OOB exfil: rare/long-label DNS callback from FHIR Java host — CVE-2026-55471 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the out-of-band exfiltration channel of the blind XXE: a parameter-entity (<!ENTITY % p SYSTEM ...>) smuggles local file contents into a DNS subdomain label, producing a first-seen external domain or an abnormally long leftmost DNS label sourced from the FHIR/Java process. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit parameter-entity OOB primitive (<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://...">) by hunting the DNS side-channel from the java process: first-seen external domain (Defender) or 30+ char leftmost label (Sentinel/Falcon/Splunk DNS-exfil heuristic). Datadog left empty — Sysmon DNS (EID 22) is not in the shipped sysmon event set. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cloud/CDN telemetry domains that use long hashed leftmost labels (telemetry, antivirus reputation lookups)
  • Legitimate Java apps doing service discovery against long auto-generated hostnames
  • First-seen anti-join firing on a newly onboarded but benign integration endpoint
  • DNS over a corporate resolver that rewrites/long-encodes names
Suppression filter
| where not(DnsQuery has_any ("akamai","cloudfront","azureedge","trafficmanager","windowsupdate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode/inspect the long DNS label — base16/base32-looking content strongly indicates file exfil; confirm the source host runs the vulnerable FHIR/Java service and correlate to a recent inbound XML POST. 2) Contain: sinkhole the parent domain at the resolver, isolate the host if the label decodes to recognizable file content, and rotate secrets the service account could read. 3) Hunt: enumerate all distinct external domains the java process queried in the last 7 days, and check the network-egress UC for the matching attacker-DTD fetch that seeded the parameter entity.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
    | where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
    | summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteUrl
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where isnotempty(DnsQuery)
| where DnsQuery !endswith "in-addr.arpa" and DnsQuery !endswith ".arpa"
| extend LeftLabel = tostring(split(DnsQuery, ".")[0])
| where strlen(LeftLabel) >= 30   // 30+ char leftmost label = data smuggled into a DNS subdomain by XXE parameter-entity OOB
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, LeftLabelLen = strlen(LeftLabel)
| order by LeftLabelLen desc

Vulnerable component exposure: org.hl7.fhir.utilities <= 6.9.9 / CVE-2026-55471 AIExploitation High
Proactive exposure hunt for hosts running the affected HAPI FHIR utilities library (vulnerable <= 6.9.9, fixed in 6.9.10) that contains the unhardened saxonTransform XXE. Surfaces the attack surface so it can be patched before exploitation. Rationale: Uses the corroborated affected package (ca.uhn.hapi.fhir:org.hl7.fhir.utilities) and CVE id (CVE-2026-55471, vulnerable <= 6.9.9, fixed 6.9.10) directly against TVM/Vulnerabilities inventory. Empty for Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch — vulnerability inventory is not part of FDR event types or the listed Datadog/CloudWatch sources. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/ca.uhn.hapi.fhir/org.hl7.fhir.utilities/CVE-2026-55471/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM reporting a transitive jar that is actually shaded/relocated and not reachable via saxonTransform
  • Dev/test build hosts with the library present but no exposed FHIR endpoint
  • Inventory lag where a host already upgraded to 6.9.10 still shows the old version until next scan
  • A vendored copy embedded in a fat-jar that TVM version-detects imprecisely
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually exposes a FHIR service that routes untrusted XML through XsltUtilities.saxonTransform (IG-publisher, validator, conversion utilities are the documented consumers) versus the library merely being on disk. 2) Contain: prioritize internet-facing FHIR servers for upgrade to org.hl7.fhir.utilities 6.9.10; where patching lags, place a WAF rule blocking XML with DOCTYPE/ENTITY on FHIR endpoints (see UC 1). 3) Hunt: for each exposed vulnerable host, run the inbound-payload, SSRF-egress, and DNS-callback UCs over the last 30 days to check for prior exploitation.

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] easy-day-js postinstall dropper spawning node.exe with C2 IP passed as argument · [LLM] Node.js writing a random 24-hex-char .js dropper to the OS temp directory · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Sapphire Sleet easy-day-js RAT C2 beacon to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Sapphire Sleet easy-day-js RAT C2 beacon to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92 / 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the two confirmed Hostwinds C2 hosts used by the Mastra/easy-day-js supply-chain RAT: 23.254.164.92:8000 (first-stage dropper download) and 23.254.164.123:443 (second-stage RAT callback). Connections from node.exe to these IPs during or shortly after an npm install are near-certain compromise. Rationale: Anchored on the two C2 IPs (23.254.164.92:8000, 23.254.164.123:443) confirmed by Microsoft, StepSecurity and JFrog as the dropper-download and RAT-callback hosts; pure IOC match so alerting-tier. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel detonation sandbox or malware-analysis VM deliberately running the sample
  • Security researcher reproducing the supply-chain attack in a lab
  • Honeypot/canary host intentionally executing the malicious package
  • Shared Hostwinds VPS range later re-allocated to a benign tenant (validate IP is still flagged before alerting long-term)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which local process opened the socket (expect node.exe) and whether an `npm install`/`npm ci` ran on the host in the prior 5 minutes; pull the parent npm command line and the user context. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node.exe RAT process tree, and block 23.254.164.92 + 23.254.164.123 at the egress proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: enumerate node_modules for easy-day-js@1.11.22 and any @mastra package at the malicious versions; rotate any developer npm tokens, browser-stored crypto-wallet seeds and session cookies on the host (RAT inventories 166 wallet extensions).
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js postinstall dropper spawning node.exe with C2 IP passed as argument AIInstallation High
Hunts the dropper's second-stage launch: setup.cjs spawns node.exe against a temp .js file passing the RAT C2 host '23.254.164.123:443' as a command-line argument. The literal C2 IP in a node command line is a near-zero-FP signal of the easy-day-js dropper. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim dropper code `child_process.spawn(process.execPath, [file, '23.254.164.123:443'])` — node.exe carrying the C2 IP as argv is an exact-string IOC, hence alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis sandbox detonating the sample
  • Lab reproduction of the attack chain by a researcher
  • Highly unlikely benign coincidence: an internal tool legitimately taking 23.254.164.123 as an argument (validate ownership before suppressing)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full process tree — expect npm/npx -> node (setup.cjs) -> node (<temp>\<hex>.js 23.254.164.123:443); note the temp script path and the spawning user. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the detached node.exe RAT, and quarantine the temp .js (it self-deletes setup.cjs, so grab it fast). 3) Hunt: search the same user/host for easy-day-js in node_modules and outbound traffic to 23.254.164.92/.123; review browser wallet-extension and history access by the RAT.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "23.254.164.123"
| where FileName =~ "node.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "23.254.164.123"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious easy-day-js package installed into node_modules AIDelivery High
Hunts the supply-chain footprint itself: files for the typosquatted easy-day-js package (a malicious dayjs clone) being written into node_modules, including its setup.cjs postinstall dropper. Presence indicates the host pulled the compromised @mastra dependency tree. Rationale: Anchored on the concrete package name `easy-day-js` (the malicious dayjs clone, v1.11.22) named in the article and every corroborating vendor write-up; the path node_modules\easy-day-js is unique to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ox.security/blog/easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-hits-mastra-ai-in-npm/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team intentionally caching the malicious package for analysis
  • SCA/registry mirror snapshotting the package for blocklisting
  • Researcher cloning the repo to study the dropper
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version is easy-day-js@1.11.22 (1.11.21 is the clean decoy) and identify which @mastra packages pulled it via ^1.11.21 caret resolution. 2) Contain: remove node_modules and lockfile, pin/forbid easy-day-js, and check for outbound 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and detached node.exe processes proving the postinstall fired. 3) Hunt: sweep all build agents/dev laptops/CI runners that ran npm install since 2026-06-16 07:05 UTC; rotate npm tokens and any secrets exposed during builds.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"node_modules\easy-day-js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"node_modules\easy-day-js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js writing a random 24-hex-char .js dropper to the OS temp directory AIInstallation Medium
Behavioural fallback that survives C2-IP rotation: detects node.exe writing a randomly-named JavaScript file (crypto.randomBytes(12) -> 24 lowercase hex chars + .js) into the OS temp directory, which is exactly how the easy-day-js postinstall stages its second-stage payload before spawning it detached. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim dropper line `path.join(os.tmpdir(), crypto.randomBytes(12).toString('hex') + '.js')` — 12 random bytes hex-encode to a 24-char lowercase pattern, a tight behavioural signature independent of the (rotatable) C2 IPs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/over-140-popular-mastra-npm-packages-hit-by-supply-chain-attack • https://research.jfrog.com/post/easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Build tools that hash-name temp scripts (some bundlers/test runners like jest/ts-node cache transforms in temp)
  • Electron/node CLI apps writing scratch scripts to temp
  • Local dev tooling generating temp ESM shims
  • AV/EDR sandbox that itself drops node temp scripts
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest","ts-node","webpack","vite","\\AppData\\Local\\Programs\\") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the temp .js still exists (the dropper self-deletes setup.cjs, often leaving the staged file briefly) and whether the writing node.exe parent is an npm install; capture the file for analysis. 2) Contain: if a detached node.exe spawned from that temp path is beaconing to 23.254.164.123, isolate the host and kill the process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate with easy-day-js in node_modules and any 23.254.164.92/.123 connections; widen to other dev hosts that ran npm install in the same window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\Temp\"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Temp\"
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"^[0-9a-f]{24}\.js$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

rclone process spawning child command (CVE-2026-49980 inline-remote RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the command-execution payload of CVE-2026-49980 / CVE-2026-41179: rclone shells out a local command during backend initialization when an unauthenticated request supplies an inline remote with a command-bearing backend option (webdav bearer_token_command or sftp ssh=). rclone is not a normal parent of arbitrary shells/binaries, so any non-rclone child of rclone on an rcd/--rc-serve host is high-fidelity. Rationale: Pivots on rclone-as-parent of any non-rclone, non-helper child — the observable end of the CVE-2026-49980 chain where a single unauthenticated GET/HEAD forces backend init to exec a local command. The PoC (bearer_token_command='/usr/bin/touch ...') confirms rclone forks an arbitrary attacker-named binary, so child name is variable but the parent is fixed; ssh/fusermount excluded as legitimate rclone backend/mount helpers. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-41179 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rclone/rclone/CVE-2026-49980/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • rclone configured with an sftp backend that uses an external ssh binary (ssh= option) for a legitimate remote — spawns ssh
  • rclone mount/serve teardown invoking fusermount/fusermount3 to unmount a FUSE volume
  • Admin-run rclone with a backend hook or wrapper script that legitimately shells out
  • Backup automation where rclone is wrapped to call a post-transfer notify command
  • Container entrypoints where rclone is PID 1 and legitimately execs a sidecar
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("ssh","ssh.exe","fusermount","fusermount3","scp","scp.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child ProcessCommandLine and the rclone InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the rclone instance is running `rcd`/`--rc-serve` without `--rc-user`/`--rc-pass`/`--rc-htpasswd`, and check whether the child is a shell/recon binary (sh, bash, id, whoami, curl) vs a known backend helper. 2) Contain: isolate the host or kill the rclone process and block inbound to its rc port (default 5572); rotate any credentials readable by the rclone process user. 3) Hunt: search the same host's web/proxy logs for inbound requests containing `bearer_token_command`/`vendor=other`, enumerate other internet-reachable rclone rc listeners, and confirm patched to >=1.74.3.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rclone","rclone.exe")
| where FileName !in~ ("rclone","rclone.exe","ssh","ssh.exe","fusermount","fusermount3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "rclone"
| where ActingProcessName endswith "rclone" or ActingProcessName endswith "rclone.exe"
| where not(TargetProcessName endswith "rclone" or TargetProcessName endswith "rclone.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "ssh" or TargetProcessName endswith "ssh.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "fusermount" or TargetProcessName endswith "fusermount3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
