Inline-remote connection-string injection in request to rclone rc (bearer_token_command) AIDelivery High
Hunts the actual CVE-2026-49980 exploit request: an unauthenticated GET/HEAD to the rclone rc listener whose URL embeds an inline remote with a command-executing backend option. The strings bearer_token_command, vendor=other and sftp,ssh= inside an HTTP request URI are not produced by normal rclone clients and are the exploit signature. Rationale: The string bearer_token_command (webdav backend) and sftp,ssh= are the exact inline backend options the GHSA/Endor PoC plants to gain code execution (fs=:webdav,...,bearer_token_command='...':). Seeing them in a request URI to the rc port (default 5572) is an unambiguous exploit attempt with essentially no benign source. Defender AH has no web-request table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jfwf-28xr-xw6q • https://www.endorlabs.com/vulnerability/cve-2026-41179 • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys/Nuclei) firing a CVE-2026-49980 template against the rc listener
  • Internal red-team / pentest engagement validating the patch
  • WAF or reverse proxy logging a blocked exploit attempt (still worth surfacing)
  • Security researchers replaying the public PoC in a lab that ships logs to prod SIEM
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei", "Nessus", "Qualys", "zgrab") and SourceIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8 scanner range — replace with your authorized scanner IPs")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract SourceIP and full RequestURL — decode the inline remote to read the command in bearer_token_command/ssh=, and determine if the rc target actually responded 200/206 (HEAD/GET serving) vs blocked. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, take the rc listener off the network or enable `--rc-user`/`--rc-pass`, and treat the host as compromised if the request reached an unpatched (<1.74.3) rclone. 3) Hunt: pivot to that host's process telemetry for an rclone-parented child (UC1) within seconds of the request, and sweep all proxy logs for the same SourceIP hitting other internal hosts on 5572.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("bearer_token_command", "vendor=other", "sftp,ssh=", ":webdav,", ":sftp,", ":local,")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed unauthenticated rclone rc deployment (rcd --rc-serve without auth) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-49980 preconditions in your own estate: rclone launched with the rc enabled (rcd/--rc-serve) and bound to a non-localhost address (--rc-addr) but missing --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd. These are the exact unauthenticated, network-reachable, file-serving deployments the advisory says are exploitable. Rationale: Encodes the advisory's stated preconditions verbatim (--rc-serve + rc reachable via --rc-addr + no --rc-user/--rc-pass/--rc-htpasswd), surfacing exploitable hosts before an attacker finds them. Localhost binds are filtered out because default rclone only serves the rc to localhost and is not remotely reachable. Cross-checked against: • https://rclone.org/commands/rclone_rcd/ • https://github.com/rclone/rclone/security/advisories/GHSA-qw24-gh76-8rvv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rclone/rclone/CVE-2026-49980/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • rclone bound to a trusted internal-only interface protected by an external firewall/security group (reachable in cmdline but not from untrusted networks)
  • Deployments that supply rc credentials via the config file or RCLONE_RC_USER/RCLONE_RC_PASS env vars instead of CLI flags (auth present but invisible to this query)
  • Short-lived rclone rcd test runs by an admin during troubleshooting
  • Hosts already patched to >=1.74.3 where the deployment is no longer exploitable
  • --rc-addr bound to a unix socket path rather than a TCP IP (not network-exposed)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr 127.0.0.1" or ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr localhost" or ProcessCommandLine has "--rc-addr unix://")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the --rc-addr value resolves to a non-loopback, internet- or untrusted-network-reachable interface and that auth is genuinely absent (check config file and RCLONE_RC_* env vars before declaring exposed). 2) Contain: add --rc-user/--rc-pass or --rc-htpasswd, or drop --rc-serve if file serving is not needed, and restrict the listener with host firewall rules; schedule upgrade to >=1.74.3. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against UC1 (rclone-parented child) and UC2 (bearer_token_command in proxy logs) to determine whether any exposed instance was already exploited.

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] LiteLLM auth bypass: malformed Host header on admin/management routes (CVE-2026-49468) · [LLM] LiteLLM unauthenticated successful write to management endpoint (CVE-2026-49468) · [LLM] LiteLLM auth bypass: 401-then-200 to same admin route with identical Host header

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

LiteLLM auth bypass: malformed Host header on admin/management routes (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation High
Hunts the root cause of CVE-2026-49468 — a crafted Host header used to make get_request_route() evaluate a different route than FastAPI dispatched. A legitimate Host is only hostname[:port]; any Host carrying a slash, '@', whitespace or '..' reaching a LiteLLM management endpoint (/key,/user,/team,...) is the injection signature. Rationale: Uses the article's exact root-cause (Host-header-driven route evaluation in get_request_route) and the confirmed LiteLLM management route prefixes (/key,/user,/team,...). A Host value containing path/@/whitespace chars is never legitimate, making this high-fidelity. defender_kql/falcon/cloudwatch/datadog empty: Defender XDR, Falcon FDR and the listed Datadog/CloudTrail sources do not ingest reverse-proxy HTTP access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/litellm/CVE-2026-49468/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/ • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1190 T1036
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Burp, OWASP ZAP, Nuclei, Nessus) deliberately fuzzing the Host header during an authorised pentest
  • A misconfigured upstream proxy that forwards a comma-joined X-Forwarded-Host chain into the Host field
  • Service-mesh / sidecar that rewrites Host to include a path-style virtual-host
  • IPv6 literal Host values bracketed oddly by a buggy client (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Nessus","Nuclei","ZAP","sqlmap","masscan") and SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.0/8"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP/Host pair; confirm the Host value is malformed (contains /,@,space,..) and which management endpoint it targeted, and whether the response was 2xx (successful bypass) vs 401/403. 2) Contain: if any 2xx returned, treat as compromise — rotate the LiteLLM master key and all virtual keys, and block the source IP at the upstream WAF/LB; confirm proxy is upgraded to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: review /key, /user, /team write operations from that source for created keys or deleted users; correlate with UC for unauthenticated admin writes and rapid state-change abuse.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/")
| where isnotempty(HttpHostName)
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[\\/@\s]" or HttpHostName contains ".."
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstHostname, DstPortNumber
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM unauthenticated successful write to management endpoint (CVE-2026-49468) AIExploitation High
Hard exploit signal for CVE-2026-49468: a state-changing request (POST/PUT/DELETE) to a LiteLLM management route (/key,/user,/team,/model,/spend,...) that returns 2xx with NO Authorization / API-key header present. These routes must never accept unauthenticated writes; a success here means the Host-header auth gate was bypassed. Rationale: Combines the article's management-route list with the invariant that these routes require an API key — a 2xx write with an empty Authorization header is the bypass success condition. Splunk CIM Web has no Authorization-header field so its SPL surfaces unauth-write candidates by method+route+2xx only (auth-header check noted as Sentinel-only); Sigma skipped because the discriminating field (absent auth header) is not in the neutral webserver schema. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch/Datadog empty — no HTTP access-log ingestion there. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://gbhackers.com/critical-litellm-flaw/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LiteLLM configured with master-key-in-cookie or session auth so the Authorization header is legitimately absent on UI-driven writes
  • Internal automation that authenticates via a custom header your log pipeline doesn't map to HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization
  • Log pipeline strips/redacts the Authorization header before indexing, making every authed request look unauthenticated
  • Health/readiness tooling that POSTs to a benign management route
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the write actually mutated state (response body / subsequent /key/list) and that no auth header or session cookie was present; verify the proxy version is <1.84.0. 2) Contain: rotate the LiteLLM master key and revoke any virtual keys created in the window; block the source IP upstream and force-upgrade to >=1.84.0 or place behind a Host-validating WAF. 3) Hunt: enumerate every object created/modified/deleted by that source across /key,/user,/team,/spend; pivot to the malformed-Host UC to confirm the injection vector and to the rapid-state-change UC for follow-on abuse.

| where HttpMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| where Url has_any ("/key/","/user/","/team/","/model/","/customer/","/spend/","/organization/")
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201","202","204")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LiteLLM auth bypass: 401-then-200 to same admin route with identical Host header AIExploitation High
Correlates a 401 followed by a 200/2xx on the SAME LiteLLM management endpoint from the SAME source IP carrying the SAME Host header value within 5 minutes. Persistence of the crafted Host value across the failed-then-successful pair proves the success was Host-header-driven (CVE-2026-49468), not a legitimate re-authentication. Rationale: Directly implements reviewer hypothesis #1: tying the 401 and the subsequent 2xx by identical SrcIpAddr + HttpHostName + route proves the same crafted Host value drove the bypass. Temporal/cross-row correlation so no Sigma. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch/Datadog empty — telemetry is reverse-proxy HTTP logs only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://cybersecuritynews.com/litellm-vulnerability-host-header-injection/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user whose API key genuinely expired, refreshed it, and retried within 5 minutes from a stable Host (legitimate re-auth)
  • Automation with a retry loop that supplies the correct key on the second attempt after a transient 401
  • Shared-NAT egress where two distinct clients reuse the same source IP and Host
  • Load-balancer health re-checks producing 401 then 200 as backends recover
Suppression filter
| where HttpHostName matches regex @"[\\/@\s]" or HttpHostName contains ".."
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the Host header value on both the 401 and the 200 — if it is malformed or differs from your canonical proxy hostname, this is the bypass; if it's the normal hostname, likely benign re-auth. 2) Contain: on confirmation, block the source IP, rotate the master key and any keys minted after the 200, and verify upgrade to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: expand the window to capture all subsequent admin actions from the source; cross-reference the unauthenticated-write and rapid-state-change UCs.

| project FailTime, OkTime, DelaySec=datetime_diff('second',OkTime,FailTime), SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, Url
| order by OkTime desc

LiteLLM recon probes (/health,/version,/docs) followed by admin-route access from same source AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects scripted exploitation of CVE-2026-49468: a source that fingerprints the proxy via /health, /version, /docs or /openapi.json and then pivots to management routes (/key,/user,/team,...) within 10 minutes. Probe-then-enumerate clustering from one source is the signature of an automated LiteLLM attack tool. Rationale: Implements reviewer hypothesis #4 using LiteLLM's real unauthenticated info routes (/health,/version,/docs,/openapi.json — present on the FastAPI proxy) and the confirmed management routes, bounded by a 10-minute window. Multi-event temporal correlation so no Sigma. Empty non-web platform fields for the same access-log reason. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes hitting /health then a monitoring job querying management routes from the same in-cluster IP
  • API gateway / uptime monitor that crawls /docs and /openapi.json for schema diffing
  • An internal developer exploring the Swagger UI then legitimately calling /key/list with a valid key
  • CI pipeline that health-checks then provisions keys during deploy
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !startswith "10." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "172.16." and SrcIpAddr !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/unexpected and that the admin-route calls lacked valid auth or returned 2xx; whitelist known monitors/CI ranges first. 2) Contain: if admin access succeeded, block the IP, rotate keys, and patch to >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: review the full request sequence for malformed Host headers (injection vector) and for any write operations; escalate to the unauthenticated-write and rapid-state-change UCs.
let recon = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where Url has_any ("/health","/version","/docs","/openapi.json")
  | project ReconTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
let admin = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

  | project AdminTime=TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode;

| where AdminTime between (ReconTime .. ReconTime + 10m)

| where match(mvjoin(uri_path,","),"/health|/version|/docs|/openapi") AND match(mvjoin(uri_path,","),"/key/|/user/|/team/")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
LiteLLM post-bypass rapid state-changing admin writes (key/user/team mutation burst) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects post-exploitation abuse after a CVE-2026-49468 bypass: a single source issuing 5+ successful state-changing writes (key generate/delete, user new/delete, team new/delete, spend/model changes) to LiteLLM management routes within a 5-minute window. This is the scripted credential-minting / account-removal stage once auth is defeated. Rationale: Implements reviewer hypothesis #5 with LiteLLM's concrete state-changing routes (/key/generate,/key/delete,/user/new,/user/delete,/team/new,...) and a 5-in-5min burst threshold for scripted abuse; mapped to T1098 (key minting), T1531 (user/key deletion), T1565 (spend/config tampering). Threshold + windowed aggregation so no Sigma. Non-web platform fields empty — access-log-only telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4xpc-pv4p-pm3w • https://deepwiki.com/BerriAI/litellm/3.5-management-endpoints-and-multi-tenancy • https://www.danilchenko.dev/posts/litellm-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1098 T1531 T1565
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bulk onboarding/offboarding automation that legitimately creates or deletes many keys/users/teams in a tight window
  • Terraform / IaC reconciliation run that mass-updates spend limits and models
  • A migration script re-provisioning virtual keys after a master-key rotation
  • Load test or QA suite exercising the management API
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["10.0.0.0"])) and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has_any ("terraform","litellm-provisioner")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the burst source carried valid auth and is an approved automation host; pull the exact objects created/deleted (new key IDs, removed users). 2) Contain: revoke all keys generated in the window, restore deleted users/teams from backup, rotate the master key, and block the source IP; verify proxy is >=1.84.0. 3) Hunt: trace the new keys' subsequent LLM usage/egress for data exfil or cost abuse, and back-correlate to the malformed-Host and unauth-write UCs to confirm the initial bypass.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE")
| where Url has_any ("/key/generate","/key/delete","/key/update","/user/new","/user/delete","/user/update","/team/new","/team/delete","/team/update","/spend/","/model/new","/model/delete")
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201","202","204")
| summarize WriteCount=count(), Endpoints=make_set(Url,30), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where WriteCount >= 5
| order by LastSeen desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_method="POST" OR Web.http_method="PUT" OR Web.http_method="DELETE") (Web.status="200" OR Web.status="201" OR Web.status="202" OR Web.status="204") (Web.uri_path="/key/generate" OR Web.uri_path="/key/delete" OR Web.uri_path="/key/update" OR Web.uri_path="/user/new" OR Web.uri_path="/user/delete" OR Web.uri_path="/team/new" OR Web.uri_path="/team/delete" OR Web.uri_path="/spend/*" OR Web.uri_path="/model/new") by Web.src Web.site _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 5
| sort - _time
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where (Web.http_method="POST" OR Web.http_method="PUT" OR Web.http_method="DELETE") (Web.status="200" OR Web.status="201" OR Web.status="202" OR Web.status="204") (Web.uri_path="/key/generate" OR Web.uri_path="/key/delete" OR Web.uri_path="/key/update" OR Web.uri_path="/user/new" OR Web.uri_path="/user/delete" OR Web.uri_path="/team/new" OR Web.uri_path="/team/delete" OR Web.uri_path="/spend/*" OR Web.uri_path="/model/new") by Web.src Web.site _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 5
| sort - _time
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-49468")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-49468")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Critical

A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope

Snyk
2026-06-16 14 use cases 7 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A dormant contributor account was used to republish the entire @mastra npm scope, each injected with a single dependency, easy-day-js, that drops a cross-platform cryptocurrency stealer. Here is how the attack worked, how to check exposure, and how to remediate.

ATT&CKT1027 T1059.001 T1176 T1190 T1195.002 T1204.002 T1555.003
Domainshwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com
IPs23.254.164.92 23.254.164.123
SHA256221c45a790dec2a2… b122a9873bedf145… c38954e85bf5433e… cdec8b20338beb70… 9570f77a5e151186…

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Node dropper fetches second stage from Hostwinds raw IP 23.254.164.92:8000
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] npm install pulls malicious easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs + .pkg marker files) · [LLM] easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) · [LLM] Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Cross-platform stealer RAT C2 beacon to 23.254.164.123 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
npm install pulls malicious easy-day-js dropper (setup.cjs + .pkg marker files) AIInstallation High
Hunts a build/dev host resolving the trojanized easy-day-js dependency: the package landing under node_modules\easy-day-js, its setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the ~/.pkg_history / ~/.pkg_logs marker files the dropper writes to track installs. Article-specific because these exact filenames and the easy-day-js package path are the carrier injected into the @mastra scope. Rationale: Anchors on the exact carrier filenames named by Snyk and corroborated by Microsoft/StepSecurity: the easy-day-js node_modules path, setup.cjs postinstall dropper, and the .pkg_history/.pkg_logs markers — none of which exist on a clean host. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox/analysis VM
  • Defenders deliberately caching the malicious tarball for IR/forensics
  • A renamed-but-unrelated package legitimately named easy-day-js in an internal registry mirror (rare)
  • Backup/EDR agents re-scanning an already-quarantined node_modules tree
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host resolved easy-day-js@1.11.21/1.11.22 — check the project lockfile and whether npm install ran on/after 2026-06-17; pull the SHA256 of any setup.cjs found. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node-spawned detached process, and treat it as credential+wallet exposure — force-reset npm tokens, cloud creds, and browser-stored secrets used on that host; revoke/rotate any wallet seed phrases. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for outbound connections to 23.254.164.92/.123 and persistence under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages; sweep CI runners and other dev laptops sharing the lockfile.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")) or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("setup.cjs",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs") or TargetFilePath has @"\node_modules\easy-day-js\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious easy-day-js npm Dropper Artifacts (Mastra Supply Chain)
id: 7c1e4d2a-9b3f-4e58-8a21-1f0c6d5b9a44
description: Detects file artifacts of the easy-day-js postinstall dropper used in the June 2026 @mastra npm scope takeover
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/a-forgotten-contributor-account-compromised-the-entire-mastra-npm-package-scope/
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/21
tags:

  - attack.t1059.007

  product: windows

  selection_markers:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\setup.cjs'

      - '\.pkg_logs'
  condition: selection_pkg or selection_markers
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\node_modules\\easy-day-js\\* OR @TargetFilename:*\\setup.cjs OR @TargetFilename:*\\.pkg_history OR @TargetFilename:*\\.pkg_logs)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| (TargetFileName=/\\node_modules\\easy-day-js\\/i OR TargetFileName=/\\setup\.cjs$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\\.pkg_history$/i OR TargetFileName=/\\\.pkg_logs$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\easy-day-js\\*" OR Filesystem.file_name="setup.cjs" OR Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_logs") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\node_modules\\easy-day-js\\*" OR Filesystem.file_name="setup.cjs" OR Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".pkg_logs") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Node dropper fetches second stage from Hostwinds raw IP 23.254.164.92:8000 AIDelivery High
Hunts the easy-day-js dropper's second-stage download: an outbound connection to the hardcoded Hostwinds host 23.254.164.92 on port 8000 (https://23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878), typically initiated by node.exe after TLS verification is disabled. High-fidelity because the IP+port are dedicated attacker infrastructure confirmed by multiple vendors. Rationale: Uses the verbatim dropper URL host/port (23.254.164.92:8000/update/49890878) from the article; Microsoft and StepSecurity independently list this as the stage-2 download endpoint, so a hit is near-certainly the dropper. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-using-easy-day-js
ATT&CKT1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation of the sample making the same fetch
  • A blue-team connectivity test confirming the IOC is reachable/blocked
  • Shared NAT egress where another tool coincidentally targets the same /24 (verify exact IP+port)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess — a node.exe/npm child reaching this IP confirms dropper execution; capture the host, user, and the resolved second-stage file in %TEMP%. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.92 at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and treat as credential+wallet compromise (rotate dev/cloud/npm tokens, browser secrets). 3) Hunt: from the same host pivot to 23.254.164.123 beacons and C:\ProgramData\NodePackages persistence; block the full 23.254.164.0/24 Hostwinds range pending review.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.92" and RemotePort == 8000
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.92" and DstPortNumber == 8000
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cross-platform stealer RAT C2 beacon to 23.254.164.123 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the second-stage crypto-stealer/RAT beaconing to its C2 at 23.254.164.123 roughly every 10 minutes over a self-signed wolfSSL channel. Aggregates repeat connections per host to surface the sustained beacon cadence rather than a single hit, distinguishing it from the one-shot dropper download. Rationale: Anchors on the article's RAT C2 IP (23.254.164.123) and the ~10-minute beacon described; the count>=3 aggregation captures the sustained cadence and filters single stray probes. No Sigma emitted because the detection is a threshold/aggregation, not a single-event shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.mend.io/blog/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-easy-day-js/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox/IR detonation of the stealer producing repeat beacons
  • Security tooling actively probing the IOC for reachability
  • Another host in the same /24 being contacted for unrelated reasons (pin to exact IP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm beacon cadence and the originating process; a ~10-min periodic connection from a non-browser process is the RAT. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 23.254.164.123 at egress, and snapshot memory before reimage; treat all secrets entered on the host as compromised. 3) Hunt: enumerate persistence (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages on Windows, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.nvm.protocal.plist on macOS, ~/.config/systemd/user/nvmconf.service on Linux) and check other hosts beaconing to the same /24.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 5), Proc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName)
            by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "23.254.164.123"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), BeaconHours=dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated),
            Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber, 5) by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr
| where ConnCount >= 3   // >=3 hits = repeat beacon, not a stray probe
| order by ConnCount desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:23.254.164.123
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="23.254.164.123"
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
| count >= 3
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count dc(_time) as distinct_times min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="23.254.164.123" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | where count >= 3 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
easy-day-js stealer persistence masquerading as Node tooling (NodePackages / LaunchAgent / systemd) AIInstallation High
Hunts the cross-platform persistence the stealer installs while disguised as Node tooling: Windows staging under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, macOS LaunchAgent com.nvm.protocal.plist, and Linux systemd user service nvmconf.service. Article-specific because these exact persistence names are unique to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three campaign-unique persistence names from the article (C:\ProgramData\NodePackages, com.nvm.protocal.plist, nvmconf.service) — the misspelled 'protocal' and 'nvmconf' are distinctive enough that a hit is effectively a true positive. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.kodemsecurity.com/resources/mastra-npm-packages-compromised-easy-day-js-supply-chain-attack-iocs-and-response-runbook

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally writing to C:\ProgramData\NodePackages (verify against the exact plist/service names)
  • Restored backup re-creating a previously-quarantined persistence file
  • IR responder copying the artifact for analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the persistence file content points to a NodePackages-staged payload or beacon; capture the writing process. 2) Contain: remove the LaunchAgent/systemd unit/Run entry, kill the persisted process, isolate the host, and rotate all credentials/wallets used there. 3) Hunt: correlate with 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and the easy-day-js install artifacts on the same and peer hosts; sweep all OS types since persistence is cross-platform.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra easy-day-js second-stage stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the obfuscated cross-platform crypto-stealer/RAT second stage by file hash on both write and execution. Hash matching is resilient to IP/infra rotation and is effectively zero-FP; the primary hash (221c45...) is the article-named stage-2 payload corroborated by Microsoft. Rationale: Primary hash 221c45a7... is the article-named second-stage payload and is corroborated by Microsoft Threat Intelligence; the additional campaign hashes are bundled IOCs. Hash matching is zero-FP and survives infrastructure rotation, complementing the IP-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/sandbox host where the sample was intentionally executed
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy retaining the hash on disk
  • Threat-intel platform caching the sample for enrichment
Response runbook
1) Triage: any hit is high-confidence malicious — confirm host, user, and whether the hash was written vs executed; the payload self-deletes, so a FileWrite without a later process may indicate cleanup. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory, and treat as full credential+wallet compromise — rotate cloud/npm/dev secrets and assume browser-stored wallet data exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot from the host to 23.254.164.92/.123 traffic and NodePackages/LaunchAgent/systemd persistence; submit the hash to org-wide retro-hunt across EDR.
let payloadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf","b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4","c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638","cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066","9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9"]);
union
( DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (payloadHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="FileWrite", Path=FolderPath, Name=FileName, SHA256,
            Proc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SHA256 in (payloadHashes)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Kind="ProcExec", Path=FolderPath, Name=FileName, SHA256,
            Proc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine )
| order by Timestamp desc
let payloadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf","b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4","c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638","cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066","9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in (payloadHashes)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123") or RemoteUrl has_any ("hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com", "hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["23.254.164.92", "23.254.164.123"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com", "hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\",
                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |
    Registry writes under the browser extension policy keys —
    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /
    info-stealers to bypass user-level extension controls.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

            - '\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\'
            - '\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\'

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d02
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers / wallet drainers read keystore files from MetaMask,
    Exodus, Atomic, Phantom, Bitcoin, Electrum, Ethereum-cli wallets.
    Filtering out the legitimate wallet binaries leaves only attacker
    activity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1005/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1005
    - attack.collection
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Ethereum\keystore\'
            - '\Bitcoin\'
            - '\Exodus\'
            - '\Electrum\wallets\'
            - '\MetaMask\'
            - '\Phantom\'
            - '\Atomic\Local Storage\'
    filter_legit:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\MetaMask.exe'
            - '\Exodus.exe'
            - '\Atomic.exe'
            - '\electrum.exe'
            - '\Bitcoin.exe'
            - '\Phantom.exe'
    condition: selection_path and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
    - Backup software
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Ethereum\keystore\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Bitcoin\wallet.dat"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Exodus\exodus.wallet*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Electrum\wallets\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\MetaMask\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Phantom\*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Atomic\Local Storage\*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("MetaMask.exe","Exodus.exe","Atomic.exe","electrum.exe","Bitcoin.exe","Phantom.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or SHA1 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9") or MD5 in~ ("221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf", "b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Article-specific bespoke detection — A Forgotten Contributor Account Compromised the Entire Mastra npm Package Scope
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,

| order by Timestamp desc

Unauthenticated POST to LobeHub /webapi/proxy from scripted/CLI User-Agent (CVE-2026-54157 SSRF) AIExploitation High
Hunts direct exploitation of the unauthenticated SSRF in LobeHub's /webapi/proxy endpoint. The article's PoC is a raw curl POST with a text/plain body; legitimate proxy traffic only originates from the LobeHub browser UI, so a POST to this exact path from curl/wget/python-requests/PowerShell is high-fidelity exploitation against a self-hosted LobeHub (<=2.1.56). Rationale: Uses the article's exact endpoint (/webapi/proxy), method (POST), and the curl-based PoC, plus the fact that every other webapi route requires checkAuth() so legit proxy traffic is browser-only. Cross-checked vs lobehub/lobe-chat#9643 which independently names the same unauthenticated endpoint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://github.com/lobehub/lobe-chat/issues/9643 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web

  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Nessus) running the CVE-2026-54157 template
  • Security team reproducing the PoC with curl during validation
  • A custom internal integration that legitimately calls the proxy via a server-side HTTP client
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has_any ("UptimeRobot","Pingdom","StatusCake","GoogleHC","kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","Datadog/Synthetics")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP and the full request; confirm the path is exactly /webapi/proxy and method POST. Check whether the LobeHub instance version is <=2.1.56 and internet-exposed. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, block the source IP at the WAF/edge and apply the fix (wrap the route in checkAuth() or remove the endpoint). Rotate Clerk session secrets if cookie reflection is suspected. 3) Hunt: review all POSTs to /webapi/proxy for the same source over 30 days, look for internal-IP/metadata targets (see related UCs) and any reflected Set-Cookie responses.

LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF targeting internal/loopback IP ranges in POST body AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts SSRF probing of internal networks through the unauthenticated /webapi/proxy. The endpoint fetches any URL supplied in the POST body server-side, so a body referencing loopback (127.0.0.1), RFC1918 ranges, or file://-style schemes indicates an attacker using LobeHub's infra to reach internal services. Requires a WAF/reverse-proxy that logs request bodies. Rationale: Builds on the article's statement that the proxy 'accepts a URL in the POST body and fetches it server-side without any authentication' (CVE-2024-32964 redirect-bypass history shows internal-network reach was the original impact). The internal-IP regex on the logged target URL is the article-specific SSRF signature; FP-prone because it depends on WAF body logging and benign internal previews. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mxhq-xw3g-rphc
ATT&CKT1190 T1046
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate URL-preview of an internal wiki/Confluence link a user pasted into LobeHub
  • WAF inspecting a body that merely mentions an RFC1918 IP in unrelated text
  • Internal pen-test / red-team validating the SSRF
  • Developer testing the proxy against localhost during deployment
Suppression filter
| where not(RequestClientApplication has_any ("Mozilla","Chrome","Safari","Edg/") and Message has "intranet-preview")
Response runbook
1) Triage: decode the POST body, confirm the fetched URL resolves to an internal/loopback target and that the response was returned (ScStatus 200). 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF, patch LobeHub (checkAuth on /webapi/proxy) and restrict egress from the LobeHub host to internal ranges. 3) Hunt: enumerate every distinct internal target the source attempted, correlate to network-layer egress from the LobeHub node process (see network-egress UC) to confirm which internal services were actually reached.

LobeHub /webapi/proxy SSRF targeting cloud metadata or internal service ports AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-theft escalation of CVE-2026-54157: a /webapi/proxy POST body pointing at the cloud instance metadata service (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) or internal datastore ports (Redis 6379, etcd 2379, Mongo 27017, Postgres 5432). On a self-hosted LobeHub running on a cloud VM with IMDSv1, this returns instance-role credentials. Includes a CloudTrail escalation query for stolen-credential reuse. Rationale: Maps the article's stated impact ('use LobeHub's infrastructure ... abusing IP-based trust') to the canonical SSRF-to-IMDS escalation. 169.254.169.254/metadata.google.internal in a proxy body is never legitimate for a chat app. The CloudWatch query surfaces EC2 instance-role credentials (session name = instance-id i-...) used from a non-internal IP, the hallmark of IMDS credential theft if LobeHub runs on EC2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A red-team validating IMDS reachability through the SSRF
  • Legitimate AssumedRole sessions from a corporate NAT egress IP not in RFC1918 (refine with your known egress CIDRs)
  • SSM/Session-Manager workflows assuming an instance role from an allow-listed bastion
  • WAF flagging a body that references a metadata IP in a non-fetch context
Suppression filter
| where not isPresent(errorCode)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the proxy body targeted 169.254.169.254/metadata and the response body (returned by the proxy) contained credential material or IAM role JSON. 2) Contain: immediately revoke/rotate the instance role's session credentials, enforce IMDSv2 (hop-limit 1, token required), block the attacker IP, and patch /webapi/proxy. 3) Hunt: run the CloudTrail query for the instance-role session name (i-...) used from any external IP in the last 30 days; review S3/STS/IAM actions performed by that session for data access.

LobeHub /webapi/proxy reflected Set-Cookie injection of Clerk session cookies AIExploitation High
Hunts the session-fixation primitive in CVE-2026-54157: the proxy passes upstream Set-Cookie headers straight through, so a POST body whose target reflects a Set-Cookie for Clerk's __session/__clerk_db_jwt/__client_uat cookies scoped to Domain=lobehub.com plants a known session value on victims. The cookie-injection payload appears verbatim in the request body. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's cookie-injection PoC: the body contains Set-Cookie + the Clerk cookie names (__session/__clerk_db_jwt/__client_uat, confirmed via Clerk docs) + Domain=lobehub.com. That triad in a /webapi/proxy body is unambiguous exploitation; no benign request reflects auth cookies through the proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://clerk.com/docs/guides/how-clerk-works/cookies
ATT&CKT1539 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the session-fixation PoC
  • A legitimate upstream that genuinely sets a __session cookie being previewed (rare; still worth investigating)
  • WAF body inspection matching the cookie name inside unrelated documentation text
  • Internal QA testing Clerk cookie behaviour through the proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the full Set-Cookie value from the body, note the planted __session value and victim scope (Domain=lobehub.com). 2) Contain: invalidate all Clerk sessions / rotate session signing keys so the fixed value is unusable, patch /webapi/proxy (checkAuth), and add a WAF rule stripping reflected Set-Cookie from proxy responses. 3) Hunt: identify any user who authenticated shortly after this request (session fixation completes at victim login) and force re-auth; review for CSRF auto-submit referers in the access logs.

LobeHub server process outbound connections to metadata/internal IPs (SSRF egress confirmation) AICommand & Control Medium
Network-layer confirmation that CVE-2026-54157 SSRF reached internal infrastructure: the LobeHub Node server process initiating connections to the cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) or internal RFC1918 hosts it would never normally contact. Excludes LobeHub's legitimate local-LLM (Ollama) and database ports to keep signal high. Rationale: Corroborates SSRF success at the network layer: a LobeHub Node process reaching 169.254.169.254 or internal hosts is anomalous for a chat app. Port exclusions (11434 Ollama, 5432 Postgres, 6379 Redis, etc.) remove LobeHub's own legitimate backend traffic so internal-probing/metadata hits stand out. Scoped via the node process + 'lobe' command-line/path hint. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2024-32964

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • LobeHub legitimately calling a self-hosted Ollama/vLLM/LM Studio on a non-excluded internal port
  • LobeHub server contacting an internal Postgres/Redis on a non-standard port
  • Container health-checks or service-mesh sidecars from the Node process
  • A self-hosted internal LLM gateway on RFC1918 that the deployment legitimately uses
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIPType in ("Private","Loopback") and RemotePort in (11434,1234,8000,5432,6379))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Node process is the LobeHub server and the internal/metadata destination is not a sanctioned backend (LLM/DB). For 169.254.169.254, treat as credential-theft attempt immediately. 2) Contain: restrict egress from the LobeHub host (deny RFC1918 + link-local except sanctioned backends), enforce IMDSv2, patch /webapi/proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to inbound /webapi/proxy POSTs on the same host/time to recover the exact attacker-supplied target URL; rotate any credentials reachable at the contacted internal service.

Exposed vulnerable LobeHub instance <=2.1.56 (CVE-2026-54157) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-exposure detection for self-hosted LobeHub running an affected version (npm:@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56) carrying the unauthenticated /webapi/proxy SSRF. Surfaces vulnerable, potentially internet-facing instances from the vulnerability inventory so they can be patched before exploitation. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete affected-package facts: CVE-2026-54157 and npm:@lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56. The Defender query joins DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to prioritise exposed instances (the SSRF is unauthenticated, so internet-facing is critical). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@lobehub/lobehub/CVE-2026-54157/
ATT&CKT1190 T1592
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lagging on a host already patched to >2.1.56 (stale inventory)
  • Air-gapped/internal-only LobeHub instances flagged as critical despite no internet exposure
  • A pinned fork that backported the checkAuth fix while reporting an old version string
  • Dev/test LobeHub container images not in production
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the running LobeHub version and whether the instance is internet-facing (IsInternetFacing/PublicIP). 2) Contain: patch to a fixed release (>2.1.56) or apply the checkAuth() wrapper / remove /webapi/proxy; place behind authenticated reverse-proxy if patch is delayed. 3) Hunt: for any instance confirmed exposed, retro-hunt its web logs for /webapi/proxy POSTs (see exploitation UCs) to determine if it was already abused before patching.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
